source_title: Bhutan GLOF creates new lake downstream, raises fears of secondary hazards - The Times of India
source_excerpt: Dehradun: A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) originating in Bhutan has prompted a flood alert across parts of Assam and West Bengal, and this has led to the formation of a new temporary lake downstream, raising concerns over a possible secondary hazard.Bhutanâs National Centre for Hydrology and Meteorology (NCHM) confirmed that the outburst led to the creation of a new artificial lake at Taktsemakhang, situated at the confluence of Sintaphu Chhu and Lungu Chhu, also known as Gangchen Tag Chhu. The newly formed body of water is being closely monitored for any potential secondary flood hazard, with NCHM advising residents along Mochhu and Punatsangchhu river valleys to remain vigilant and avoid riverbanks and low-lying areas.The Oct 29 outburst originated from Shintaphu glacial lake, which was estimated to have contained around six million cubic metres of water prior to the breach. Indiaâs Central Water Commission (CWC) subsequently issued a special flood advisory for West Bengal and Assam, warning that water levels in Alipurduar and Dhubri districts could rise sharply as floodwaters move downstream through Sankosh river system.According to International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), before the outburst, Sintaphu Lake was estimated to contain 6 to 7 million cubic metres of water, equivalent to approximately 2,400â2,800 Olympic-sized swimming pools. The volume of water released remains under assessment.Ashim Sattar, a glacial hazard expert at IIT Bhubaneswar, told TOI that the formation of temporary lakes downstream is a known risk during such disasters. âDuring GLOFs, powerful floodwaters erode river valleys and carry large amounts of debris, which can temporarily block river channels and form new lakes. Such lakes generally drain naturally, but they can also become secondary flood hazards if they are not regularly monitored,â Sattar said.He explained that Shintaphu was a medium-sized glacial lake located close to Lunana glacial lake complexâa cluster of four lakes including Thorthormi, which is considered one of Bhutanâs most hazardous.According to NCHM, the flood crossed Taktsemakhang around 8:27 pm on Thursday. Warning sirens along Mochhu and downstream Punatsangchhu were activated as monitoring stations recorded a sharp rise in river levels. At Yebesa, the water level peaked at 6.7 m at 11 pm before receding to a normal level of 2.84 m around 12:30 am on Fridayâa drop of 3.86 m within 90 minutes.Sattar noted that the timely activation of the regional early-warning network prevented loss of life. âThe early-warning system was in place and was activated on time, allowing people in vulnerable areas to take precautions. This played an important role in ensuring that there were no casualties,â he said.The incident highlights the growing threat of cascading disasters in the Himalayas, where an initial glacial breach can trigger secondary hazards downstream through valley erosion, sediment deposition and temporary river blockages.Previous assessments by ICIMOD and UNDP identified 47 major potentially dangerous glacial lakes (PDGLs) across the transboundary Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins. Current estimates show that 388 GLOFs have been documented across HKH, including Karakoram, Central and Eastern Himalaya.In 2015, a GLOF in the headwaters of Mo Chuu river, where Sintaphu Lake is located, prompted Bhutanese authorities to work with SERVIR-Himalaya initiative to assess glacial lake risks in the catchment, according to experts at ICIMOD.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news.
